safetyNote: Agaricus silvicola is listed as edible by DGfM and VAPKO, but its pale young gills and white cap invite dangerous confusion with deadly white Amanita species. Other yellowing Agaricus, including the toxic A. xanthodermus, are also lookalikes. Never eat a wild specimen from this plate or app alone: retain the complete stem base and seek expert identification. DGfM warns that yellowing agarics, including this species, may accumulate high cadmium concentrations; avoid contaminated collecting sites.

sections.title: Identification
sections.text: The wood mushroom has a white to ivory cap, usually about 5–12 cm across, initially globose, then convex to broad and flatter. Its surface is smooth to finely silky or fibrillose, and slowly develops pale yellow to ochre tones where rubbed or as it ages. The outline can be graceful and relatively slender for a large Agaricus. The pleasant aniseed or almond-like odour is useful but should be checked with other characters.

sections.title: Gills, ring and base
sections.text: The crowded gills are free from the stem. They may be very pale in a young fruit body, then become greyish pink and finally chocolate to dark brown as the spores mature. The white to yellow-grey stem is roughly 5–12 cm tall, often with a slight to modest basal bulb but no volva. A broad, membranous, hanging ring sits high on the stem; it may yellow with age and can be woolly or floccose below. The spore deposit is chocolate brown.

sections.title: Flesh and ecology
sections.text: The flesh is white and generally changes little when cut, sometimes showing a slight pinkish tinge in the upper stem. Yellowing is most useful on the cap or stem surface after handling, not as a universal bright-yellow cut-flesh reaction. This saprobic species grows in small groups or scattered individuals on woodland litter in both conifer and broadleaf woods. In temperate Europe it fruits mainly from late summer into autumn, with regional variation.

sections.title: Lookalikes and contamination
sections.text: A. xanthodermus tends to stain rapidly chrome yellow at the stem base when cut and often smells of ink, iodine or phenol rather than aniseed; the Swiss VAPKO list specifically flags this confusion. White or pale Amanita phalloides, A. virosa and A. verna retain white gills at maturity and have a volva, which may be buried in soil. A closed young Agaricus can also have pale gills, so inspect developed specimens and the entire base. The DGfM specifically names A. silvicola among yellowing agarics that can contain much cadmium, reinforcing the need to avoid polluted ground.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The white-background plate shows a complete pale woodland fruit body with a slender stem, modest bulb and broad hanging ring; a cap top with gentle yellow ageing; a lengthwise section with white flesh; and an underside view showing free gills progressing from pale pink to brown. It represents recognition features rather than an edibility test.
